purpose: Project-linked conversations extending beyond the writer history window; actual facts, hypothetical corrections and topic switches must stay separate.

questions: For this proposed new Group B office building, the room has 30 occupants. Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, does that occupant count alone require its egress door to swing in the direction of egress travel?
Suppose the same room has 80 occupants instead. Would the swing-direction requirement change? Keep this as a hypothetical, not a change to our actual project.
Actually, make that 90 occupants in the hypothetical room. What is the result?
For that same hypothetical room, explain the direction of egress travel in plain language.
For the same hypothetical case, would sprinklers alone waive the occupant-load door-swing requirement?
Would a wider door alone waive that swing-direction requirement in the same hypothetical?
Please give the code section supporting the swing-direction answer for that hypothetical room.
For that same hypothetical room, is swing direction the same issue as clear opening width? Keep it brief.
For the same hypothetical case, explain why satisfying one door requirement is not a complete door-compliance determination.
What occupant count are we currently assuming for the hypothetical room, and is that a confirmed change to the actual project?
Back to the actual project: use the occupant count I originally gave for the room. Does that count alone trigger the swing-direction rule?
New topic: under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, are S-traps permitted?
Return to the original actual office-room door question. What occupant count was confirmed, and what is the limited conclusion about swing direction?
checks: 30 below 75; no occupant-count-alone trigger; not full door approval
Sprinklers do not waive the 75-person trigger
Actual 30 and limited no-trigger result recovered

questions: For this project, consider a Class A portable fire extinguisher. The actual travel distance is 60 feet. Under the 2022 NYC Fire Code, does that meet the maximum travel-distance limit? Limit the answer to that distance.
Suppose the travel distance is 90 feet instead. Keep this as a hypothetical scenario; does that distance satisfy the limit?
Correction within the hypothetical: the travel distance is 80 feet, not 90 feet. Does that change the result?
For the same hypothetical Class A case, should we use the walking route or a straight-line measurement through walls?
For the same hypothetical case, would a clear line of sight to the extinguisher by itself waive the travel-distance limit?
Does using a bigger extinguisher automatically remove that travel-distance maximum in this hypothetical?
For this same hypothetical case, cite the section or table for the Class A travel-distance maximum.
Explain briefly why extinguisher rating and travel distance are separate checks for this hypothetical.
For that same hypothetical, give a short drawing-review note focused only on the travel distance.
What travel distance are we currently assuming in the hypothetical, and did I confirm it as a change to the actual project?
Back to the actual project: use the travel distance I originally gave. Does that distance meet the Class A maximum?
New topic: under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code, can gas piping run through a ducted supply-air duct?
Return to the original actual Class A extinguisher question. What was the actual travel distance and the limited conclusion?
checks: FC 906.3.1 and Table 906.3.1 or accurate parent citation
FGC 404.3 duct prohibition; no extinguisher contamination
Actual 60 and limited within-75 result recovered

questions: Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, consider mechanical exhaust for one private dwelling-unit bathroom. Our actual proposal is 25 cfm operated continuously. Does that meet the table minimum exhaust rate? Limit the conclusion to that airflow rate.
Suppose the same bathroom instead exhausts 15 cfm continuously. This is a hypothetical, not a change to our actual proposal. Does it meet that rate?
Correction within the hypothetical: use 10 cfm continuously, not 15 cfm. Does the correction change the result?
For that same hypothetical, explain what continuous operation means in plain language.
For the same private bathroom, does the table use a different minimum rate for intermittent operation?
Keep the hypothetical at 10 cfm continuous. Would switching that same 10 cfm fan to intermittent operation make it meet the table rate?
For the same hypothetical private bathroom, which table and footnote support the continuous versus intermittent rates?
For that hypothetical, explain briefly why operating mode and airflow rate must be checked together.
For the same hypothetical, give a brief drawing-review note about the airflow shortfall only.
What airflow rate and operating mode are we currently assuming in the hypothetical, and did I confirm a change to the actual project?
Back to the actual project: use the airflow rate and operating mode I originally gave. Does it meet the table rate?
New topic: under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code, is a supply-air duct an allowed location for gas piping?
Return to the original actual private-bathroom exhaust proposal. State its airflow, mode and limited table-rate result.
checks: 25 cfm continuous meets 20 cfm minimum, not full design approval
10 cfm still below 20; correction does not change failure
Continuous operation explained without inventing duty cycle
10 cfm below either minimum; changing mode does not fix rate
MC Table 403.3.1.1 and footnote f or accurate parent with footnote meaning
Mode determines which minimum; 10 cfm below continuous threshold
10 cfm is 10 below continuous 20 minimum, no full approval
Hypothetical 10 cfm continuous, actual 25 cfm continuous
FGC 404.3 supply duct prohibited; no airflow contamination
Actual 25 continuous and limited meets20 recovered

corrections: Door swing: NYC BC 1010.1.2.2 uses 75 occupants, not the generic IBC 50-person threshold. Questions unchanged; earlier runs preserved.
NYC FC Class A table reference is Table 906.3.1, not generic IFC Table 906.3(1).
Private dwelling bathroom rates are per room under footnote f (not public-toilet footnote e); continuous means while the dwelling or sleeping unit is occupied.
